claims.evidence: Direct statement of total cell count in the dataset

claims.claim: Twenty-one cell types were identified with Leiden clustering and manual merging.
claims.source: Twenty-one cell types were identified with Leiden clustering and manual merging and visualized using Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP; Figure 1B; Table 2).
claims.evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 1B and Table 2

claims.claim: Samples from patients who had been diagnosed with T1D for 0–2 years had significantly reduced β-cell frequencies compared to non-T1D controls.
claims.source: Similarly, we found that samples from patients who had been diagnosed with T1D for 0–2 years had significantly reduced β-cell frequencies compared to non-T1D controls.
claims.evidence: Direct statement of statistical finding

claims.claim: Samples from subjects with disease durations of 5–6 years had minimal remaining β-cell mass.
claims.source: Furthermore, samples from subjects with disease durations of 5–6 years had minimal remaining β-cell mass (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 1D

claims.claim: Donors were clearly separated into two groups by the first two principal components based on the abundances of non-endocrine cell types located in islets.
claims.source: We performed Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on the donors using the frequencies of non-endocrine cell types located in islets. Donors were clearly separated into two groups by the first two principal components; one group included all T1D cases and one AA+ case and the second included all non-T1D cases and the other AA+ case (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: Direct statement of PCA results with reference to Figure 1E

claims.claim: Both the islet and extra-islet spaces of T1D and non-T1D cases were distinct.
claims.source: Therefore, both the islet and extra-islet spaces of T1D and non-T1D cases were distinct.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from PCA analysis of both compartments

claims.claim: In human T1D, β-cell destruction does not occur simultaneously across all islets.
claims.source: In human T1D, β-cell destruction does not occur simultaneously across all islets and even neighboring islets can be at different stages of destruction (Damond et al., 2019; In't Veld, 2014; In't Veld, 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Damond et al., 2019; In't Veld, 2014; In't Veld, 2011

claims.claim: Pseudotime analysis using PAGA identified a continuum from islets abundant in insulin-expressing β-cells to islets depleted in β-cells.
claims.source: In the PAGA map, a continuum is apparent from islets abundant in insulin-expressing β-cells on the left of the map to islets depleted in β-cells on the right (Figure 2D, Figure 2E, Figure 2F, top row).
claims.evidence: Direct statement with reference to multiple figures showing the continuum

claims.claim: Islets were labeled into three groups: Normal, Inflamed, and Insulin-Depleted based on PAGA-internal Leiden clustering.
claims.source: PAGA uses Leiden clustering internally, enabling the following regions of the pseudotime map to be labeled objectively: (1) Islets with low pseudotime values on the left of the map (PAGA-internal Leiden clusters 0 and 5 in Figure 2—figure supplement 1) were labeled 'Normal' even if they originated from T1D donors. (2) Islets in the middle of the map (PAGA-internal Leiden clusters 6, 2, and 8 in Figure 2—figure supplement 1) were elevated in HLA-ABC (MHC Class I) expression, CD8+T cells, and macrophage/DCs (Figure 2D, Figure 2E, Figure 2F, rows 2–4) and were labeled 'Inflamed'. (3) Islets with late pseudotime values on the right of the map (PAGA-internal Leiden clusters 1, 3, 7, and 4 in Figure 2—figure supplement 1) were devoid of β-cells and were labeled 'Insulin-Depleted' (Figure 2D, Figure 2E, Figure 2F, top row).
claims.evidence: Direct statement of classification method with references to figures

claims.claim: Inflamed islets were elevated in HLA-ABC (MHC Class I) expression, CD8+T cells, and macrophage/DCs.
claims.source: Islets in the middle of the map (PAGA-internal Leiden clusters 6, 2, and 8 in Figure 2—figure supplement 1) were elevated in HLA-ABC (MHC Class I) expression, CD8+T cells, and macrophage/DCs (Figure 2D, Figure 2E, Figure 2F, rows 2–4) and were labeled 'Inflamed'.
claims.evidence: Direct statement with reference to figures showing elevated markers

claims.claim: Immune cells were targeting islets specifically, as demonstrated by increased fractions of B cells, CD4+T cells, CD8+T cells, macrophage/DCs, neutrophils, and plasma cells in islets relative to outside the islets.
claims.source: We quantified the fraction of each cell type in swaths at varying distances from the islet edge. We found that for B cells, CD4+T cells, CD8+T cells, macrophage/DCs, neutrophils, and plasma cells, the fraction of the given cell type in the islet relative to outside the islets increased (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), demonstrating that the inflammation in islets was distinct from the inflammation in the extra-islet tissue. Thus, immune cells were targeting islets specifically.
claims.evidence: Direct statement based on spatial analysis with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claims.claim: The results illustrate a single, non-branching progression from Normal Islets to Insulin-Depleted Islets via Inflamed Islets.
claims.source: Together, these results illustrate a single, non-branching progression from Normal Islets to Insulin-Depleted Islets via Inflamed Islets, consistent with previous pseudotime analyses (Damond et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from pseudotime analysis, supported by citation to Damond et al., 2019

claims.claim: IDO expression on islet vasculature was observed in islets.
claims.source: We observed islets in which CD31+ vasculature stained positive for indoleamine 2, 3-dioxygenase 1 (IDO).
claims.evidence: Direct observation from imaging data

claims.claim: In islets, IDO did not co-stain with CD45+ immune cells adjacent to vasculature.
claims.source: In islets, IDO did not co-stain with CD45+ immune cells adjacent to vasculature (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: Direct observation from imaging data shown in Figure 2G

claims.claim: IDO expression was not observed in endocrine or other cell types in islets or in vasculature or any cell type outside islets.
claims.source: We did not observe IDO expression in endocrine or other cell types in islets or in vasculature or any cell type outside islets (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: Direct observation from imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5

claims.claim: All but two IDO+ islets were in the Inflamed group.
claims.source: We manually quantified vascular expression of IDO in islets throughout pseudotime and found that all but two IDO+ islets were in the Inflamed group (Figure 2H).
claims.evidence: Direct statement of quantification results shown in Figure 2H

claims.claim: IDO expression by islet vasculature was tightly associated with insulitis.
claims.source: Therefore, IDO expression by islet vasculature was tightly associated with insulitis.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from the observation that IDO+ islets were predominantly in the Inflamed group

claims.claim: CD8+T cells were significantly more abundant in islets with IDO+ vasculature than islets without IDO+ vasculature.
claims.source: We compared the frequency of CD8+T cells and macrophage/DCs in islets from the Inflamed group with and without IDO+ vasculature and found that CD8+T cells were significantly more abundant in islets with IDO+ vasculature than islets without IDO+ vasculature (Figure 2I).
claims.evidence: Direct statement of statistical comparison shown in Figure 2I

claims.claim: The expression of HLA-ABC was higher in β-cells in IDO+ islets than in β-cells in IDO– islets.
claims.source: In addition, the expression of HLA-ABC, another interferon-stimulated gene, was higher in β-cells in IDO+ islets than in β-cells in IDO– islets (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
claims.evidence: Direct statement of comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6

claims.claim: The abundance of macrophage/DCs was not significantly associated with IDO+ vasculature.
claims.source: However, the abundance of γδ-T cells and CD4+T cells was less strongly associated with IDO+ vasculature and the abundance of macrophage/DCs was not significantly associated with IDO+ vasculature (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
claims.evidence: Direct statement of statistical finding shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6

claims.claim: IDO expression by islet vasculature is positively associated with T cell infiltration and may be an immunoregulatory checkpoint in T1D.
claims.source: In summary, IDO expression by islet vasculature is positively associated with T cell infiltration and may be an immunoregulatory checkpoint in T1D.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from the association between IDO+ vasculature and CD8+T cell abundance

claims.claim: A neural network was trained on manually labeled images of single T cells to quantify the expression of T cell markers on islet CD8+T cells.
claims.source: To obtain extremely high-quality marker quantification, we trained a neural network on manually labeled images of single T cells (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1). Using our neural network, we quantified the expression of T cell markers on islet CD8+T cells (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: Direct statement of methodology with references to figures

claims.claim: PD-1, TOX, CD45RO, CD69, and CD44, markers of antigen experience, were the markers most frequently expressed by islet-infiltrating CD8+T cells.
claims.source: PD-1, TOX, CD45RO, CD69, and CD44, markers of antigen experience, were the markers most frequently expressed by islet-infiltrating CD8+T cells (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Direct statement with reference to figures showing marker expression

claims.claim: CD8+T cells expressing CD45RA were detectable in islets.
claims.source: CD8+T cells expressing CD45RA (which are either naive or terminally differentiated effector memory cells [TEMRA]) were detectable in islets, as previously reported (Damond et al., 2019; Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: Direct observation with reference to Figure 3B and citation to Damond et al., 2019

claims.claim: A rare population of CD45RO+/CD8+T cells co-expressing LAG-3, Granzyme-B, and ICOS was observed.
claims.source: In addition, we observed a rare population of CD45RO+/CD8+T cells co-expressing LAG-3, Granzyme-B, and ICOS (P bottom clade).
claims.evidence: Direct observation from marker expression analysis

claims.claim: A rare population of CD57+/CD8+T cells was present but these cells rarely co-expressed LAG-3, Granzyme-B, or ICOS.
claims.source: Lastly, a rare population of CD57+/CD8+T cells was present but these cells rarely co-expressed LAG-3, Granzyme-B, or ICOS (Figure 3B top clade).
claims.evidence: Direct observation from marker expression analysis shown in Figure 3B

claims.claim: The activation profiles of islet-infiltrating T cells are heterogeneous.
claims.source: Therefore, the activation profiles of islet-infiltrating T cells are heterogeneous.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from the observation of multiple distinct T cell populations

claims.claim: Four inflamed sub-clusters (I–IV) were identified based on the frequencies of CD8+T cells expressing each functional marker.
claims.source: To interrogate this, we performed UMAP only on Inflamed islets, using the frequencies of CD8+T cells expressing each functional marker. We identified four inflamed sub-clusters, I–IV, (Figure 3C top).
claims.evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 3C

claims.claim: Inflamed-I contained only CD8+T cells that did not express any of the functional markers analyzed.
claims.source: Inflamed-I contained only CD8+T cells that did not express any of the functional markers analyzed (Figure 3C bottom, top row).
claims.evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 3C

claims.claim: Inflamed-II was characterized by a high frequency of CD45RA+/CD8+T cells.
claims.source: Inflamed-II was characterized by a high frequency of CD45RA+/CD8+T cells (Figure 3C bottom, second row from top and Figure 3D top row).
claims.evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figures 3C and 3D

claims.claim: Inflamed-III was characterized by a low frequency of CD45RA+ cells and high frequency of CD45RO+ and PD-1+ cells.
claims.source: Inflamed-III was characterized by a low frequency of CD45RA+ cells and high frequency of CD45RO+ and PD-1+ cells (Figure 3C bottom, third row from top and Figure 3D middle row).
claims.evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figures 3C and 3D

claims.claim: Inflamed-IV was characterized by an enrichment of CD8+T cells expressing CD57, LAG-3, ICOS, Granzyme-B, PD-1 or CD45RO.
claims.source: Inflamed-IV was characterized by an enrichment of CD8+T cells expressing CD57, LAG-3, ICOS, Granzyme-B, PD-1 or CD45RO (Figure 3C bottom, bottom row and Figure 3D bottom row).
claims.evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figures 3C and 3D

claims.claim: The phenotypes of CD8+T cells are coordinated across islets.
claims.source: In summary, the phenotypes of CD8+T cells are coordinated across islets.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from the identification of distinct inflamed sub-clusters

claims.claim: Each donor possessed islets that belonged to multiple inflamed islet sub-clusters.
claims.source: To identify cellular or molecular factors that regulate the state of CD8+T cells in islets, we first inspected the distribution of inflamed sub-clusters in each patient. Each donor possessed islets that belonged to multiple inflamed islet sub-clusters (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 3E

claims.claim: Donor-level factors such as genetics, the location within the pancreas, or time since T1D onset are not associated with inflamed sub-clusters.
claims.source: Therefore donor-level factors such as genetics, the location within the pancreas (i.e. head, body, or tail), or time since T1D onset, are not associated.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from the observation that each donor had multiple sub-clusters

claims.claim: Insulitis sub-states are conserved among T1D patients.
claims.source: Instead, these insulitis sub-states are conserved among T1D patients.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from the observation that sub-clusters are present across multiple donors

claims.claim: For islets of Inflamed-II, -III, and -IV, functional markers characterizing their CD8+T cells were expressed more frequently inside than in the surrounding tissue areas.
claims.source: We found that for islets of Inflamed-II, -III, and -IV, functional markers characterizing their CD8+T cells were expressed more frequently inside than in the surrounding tissue areas.
claims.evidence: Direct statement of spatial analysis results

claims.claim: The specific differences in the compositions of CD8+T cell states in different islets were attributable to the islet microenvironment and not the surrounding extra-islet spaces.
claims.source: This demonstrated that the specific differences in the compositions of CD8+T cell states in different islets were attributable to the islet microenvironment and not the surrounding extra-islet spaces.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from spatial analysis showing enrichment of markers inside islets

claims.claim: Neither the expression of markers of macrophage/DC activity nor macrophage/DC abundance was significantly associated with any of the inflamed sub-clusters.
claims.source: Although macrophage/DCs are abundant in islets from the Inflamed group (Figure 2E, Figure 2F) and can interact with T cells by presenting antigen or secreting cytokines, neither the expression of markers of macrophage/DC activity nor macrophage/DC abundance was significantly associated with any of the inflamed sub-clusters (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: Direct statement of statistical finding shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4

claims.claim: No other cell type nor the vascular expression of IDO was linked to CD8+T cell programs in islets.
claims.source: Similarly, no other cell type nor the vascular expression of IDO was linked to CD8+T cell programs in islets (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: Direct statement of statistical finding shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4

claims.claim: The activation states of islet-infiltrating T cells are independent of the abundance of any of the other cell types identified.
claims.source: Accordingly, the four inflamed sub-clusters had identical distributions throughout the original PAGA force-directed layout (Figure 3F). Therefore, the activation states of islet-infiltrating T cells are independent of the abundance of any of the other cell types we could identify.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from the observation that sub-clusters had identical distributions in pseudotime, shown in Figure 3F

claims.claim: Insulin-Depleted + Immune islets contained a higher frequency of CD45RA+/CD8+T cells and a lower frequency of CD45RO+/CD8+T cells than Inflamed islets.
claims.source: Lastly, we compared CD8+T cells in islets from the Insulin-Depleted + Immune group to CD8+T cells in islets from the Inflamed group. Insulin-Depleted + Immune islets contained a higher frequency of CD45RA+/CD8+T cells and a lower frequency of CD45RO+/CD8+T cells than Inflamed islets (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: Direct statement of comparison shown in Figure 3G

claims.claim: TOX was expressed by a higher frequency of CD8+T cells in Insulin-Depleted + Immune islets than CD8+T cells in Inflamed islets.
claims.source: TOX was expressed by a higher frequency of CD8+T cells in Insulin-Depleted + Immune islets than CD8+T cells in Inflamed islets (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: Direct statement of comparison shown in Figure 3G

claims.claim: CD45RA and TOX were never co-expressed on the same CD8+T cell.
claims.source: Importantly, CD45RA and TOX were never co-expressed on the same CD8+T cell (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: Direct observation from marker expression analysis shown in Figure 3B

claims.claim: The activation state or persistence of CD45RA+ and TOX+ CD8+T cell populations in islets depends on insulin expression.
claims.source: These data indicate that the activation state or persistence of these two populations in islets depends on insulin expression.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from the differences in CD45RA+ and TOX+ T cells between Inflamed and Insulin-Depleted + Immune islets

claims.claim: In the pancreas, islets are grouped within lobules.
claims.source: In the pancreas, islets are grouped within lobules.
claims.evidence: Statement of anatomical organization

claims.claim: In some donors, the destruction of islets in T1D exhibits a strong lobular patterning.
claims.source: In some donors, the destruction of islets in T1D exhibits a strong lobular patterning: that is, insulin-positive, immune-infiltrated, and insulin-negative islets are each primarily found in different lobules (Gepts, 1965).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Gepts, 1965

claims.claim: The intra-class correlation coefficient (ICC) was used to quantify the degree of lobular patterning within each donor.
claims.source: To systematically investigate lobular patterning in T1D, we used a neural network to segment lobules and assign each single cell and islet to its lobule. We first quantified the degree of lobular patterning within each donor using the intra-class correlation coefficient (ICC).
claims.evidence: Direct statement of methodology

claims.claim: In the remaining cases (excluding non-T1D cases and cases 6314, 6195, and 6323), the ICCs ranged from 0.17 to 0.74.
claims.source: Islets of non-T1D cases and 6314, 6195, and 6323 did not have appreciable variability in their pseudotimes, but in the remaining cases, the ICCs ranged from 0.17 to 0.74 (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: Direct statement of ICC values shown in Figure 4B

claims.claim: The magnitude of lobular patterning ranges widely across T1D cases with insulitis.
claims.source: This highlights that the magnitude of lobular patterning ranges widely across T1D cases with insulitis.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from the range of ICC values

claims.claim: Three cell types — vasculature, nerves, and Granzyme-B+/CD3- cells — were significantly associated with lobules across multiple T1D tissue donors.
claims.source: We identified three cell types — vasculature, nerves, and Granzyme-B+/CD3- cells — that were significantly associated with lobules across multiple T1D tissue donors.
claims.evidence: Direct statement of hierarchical linear modeling results

claims.claim: Vasculature, Granzyme-B+/CD3- cells, and nerves were all more abundant in lobules with islets late in pseudotime.
claims.source: All three were more abundant in lobules with islets late in pseudotime (Figure 4C boxed rows, Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figures 4C and 4D

claims.claim: Samples from cases 6323 and 6195 had increased abundances of vasculature, Granzyme-B+/CD3- cells, and nerves in their extra-islet spaces compared to non-T1D controls.
claims.source: Samples from cases 6323 and 6195 which had very few insulin-containing islets had increased abundances of vasculature, Granzyme-B+/CD3- cells, and nerves in their extra-islet spaces compared to non-T1D controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), indicating these changes persist through the point when the entire tissue is afflicted.
claims.evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claims.claim: Vasculature, Granzyme-B+/CD3- cells, and nerves were increased in Inflamed islets compared to Normal islets.
claims.source: In addition, vasculature, Granzyme-B+/CD3- cells, and nerves were increased in Inflamed islets compared to Normal islets indicating that they may serve a role in islets in addition to their role in the extra-islet compartment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claims.claim: Although CD8+T cells and macrophage/DCs were higher in the extra-islet compartments of T1D cases vs non-T1D cases, they were not associated with lobular patterning.
claims.source: Counterintuitively, although CD8+T cells and macrophage/DCs were higher in the extra-islet compartments of T1D cases vs non-T1D cases (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), they were not associated with lobular patterning (they were not more abundant in the extra-islet space of lobules with more advanced insulitis; Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: Direct statement with references to Figures 1—figure supplement 3 and 4C

claims.claim: Vasculature, Granzyme-B/CD3- cells, and nerves outside islets may help predispose lobules to insulitis or are affected by extensive insulitis.
claims.source: These data raise the possibility that vasculature, Granzyme-B/CD3- cells, and nerves outside islets help predispose lobules to insulitis or are affected by extensive insulitis.
claims.evidence: Speculative conclusion drawn from the association between these cell types and lobular patterning

claims.claim: Cellular neighborhoods (CNs) were identified by clustering single cells according to the cell type composition of their twenty nearest spatial neighbors.
claims.source: Therefore, we identified cellular neighborhoods (CNs; Schürch et al., 2020; Bhate et al., 2022), tissue regions that are homogeneous and have defined cell type compositions. To identify CNs, single cells were clustered according to the cell type composition of their twenty nearest spatial neighbors and automatically annotated with the names of enriched cell types (Figure 5A, See Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: Direct statement of methodology with reference to Figure 5A and citations

claims.claim: 75 cellular neighborhoods (CNs) were identified.
claims.source: This resulted in 75 CNs.
claims.evidence: Direct statement of the number of CNs identified

claims.claim: The top three CNs (by fold change of abundance in T1D relative to non-T1D) were (CD8+T cells|B cells), (Macrophage|Stromal Cells|B cells), and (Vasculature|B cells).
claims.source: Next, we identified CNs that were more abundant in T1D than non-T1D tissues (Figure 5B). The top three CNs (fold change of abundance in T1D relative to abundance in non-T1D) were (CD8+T cells|B cells), (Macrophage|Stromal Cells|B cells), and (Vasculature|B cells) (Figure 5B, Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figures 5B and 5C

claims.claim: The (CD8+T cells|B cells) CN is predominantly found adjacent to both (Macrophage|Stroma|B cells) and (Vasculature|B cells) CNs.
claims.source: Measuring the frequency with which the three B cell CNs were adjacent to each other throughout the tissues demonstrated that the (CD8+T cells|B cells) CN is predominantly found adjacent to both the other CNs but that (Macrophage|Stroma|B cells) and (Vasculature|B cells) are less commonly adjacent to each other (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 5D

claims.claim: The (CD8+T cells|B cells) CN was not in the perivascular space.
claims.source: Although the (CD8+T cells|B cells) CN was adjacent to vessels (Figure 5D, Figure 5E), it was not in the perivascular space, as is the case with perivascular cuffs (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: Direct observation from imaging data shown in Figures 5D and 5E

claims.claim: The (CD8+T cells|B cells) CN did not have segregated T cell and B cell zones as seen in mature TLSs.
claims.source: In our samples, the (CD8+T cells|B cells) CN did not have segregated T cell and B cell zones as seen in mature TLSs, consistent with previous reports (Korpos et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Direct observation with citation to Korpos et al., 2021

claims.claim: The (CD8+T cells|B cells) CN is more abundant in T1D tissues from patients with diabetes durations of 0–2 years compared to non-T1D tissues and T1D tissue from patients who had T1D for more than 4 years.
claims.source: In summary, the (CD8+T cells|B cells) CN is more abundant in T1D tissues from patients with diabetes durations of 0–2 years compared to non-T1D tissues and T1D tissue from patients who had T1D for more than 4 years.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from CN abundance analysis

claims.claim: PNAd expression was observed in the vessels associated with the (CD8+T cells|B cells) CN.
claims.source: We observed expression of peripheral lymph node addressin (PNAd), an HEV marker, in the vessels associated with the (CD8+T cells|B cells) CN (Figure 5E left image) but not in other vessels (data not shown).
claims.evidence: Direct observation from imaging data shown in Figure 5E

claims.claim: Instances of the (CD8+T cells|B cells) CN are immature TLSs.
claims.source: Although we could not assess the presence of other TLS traits such as follicular dendritic cells, fibroblastic reticular cells, or follicular helper T cells, the aggregation of B cells and presence of HEVs, but the lack of compartmentalized B and T cell zones indicate that instances of the (CD8+T cells|B cells) CN are immature TLSs.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from the presence of B cells, HEVs, and lack of segregated zones

claims.claim: CD8+T cells co-expressing CD45RA and CD62L were observed near PNAd+ vasculature.
claims.source: Next, we asked if immature TLSs could support the entry of naive CD8+T cells into the pancreas. We observed CD8+T cells co-expressing CD45RA and CD62L (the ligand for PNAd) near PNAd+ vasculature (Figure 5E, middle and right image respectively).
claims.evidence: Direct observation from imaging data shown in Figure 5E

claims.claim: CD45RA+/CD8+T cells in the pancreas may adhere to HEVs.
claims.source: Thus, CD45RA+/CD8+T cells in the pancreas may adhere to HEVs.
claims.evidence: Inference drawn from the observation of CD45RA+/CD62L+/CD8+T cells near PNAd+ vasculature

claims.claim: CD45RA+ was enriched threefold on CD8+T cells in the (CD8+T cells|B cells) CN relative to CD8+T cells in the tissue as a whole.
claims.source: Furthermore, CD45RA+ was enriched threefold on CD8+T cells in the (CD8+T cells|B cells) CN relative to CD8+T cells in the tissue as a whole (Figure 5F), providing additional evidence that CD45RA+ T cells may enter the pancreas through HEVs.
claims.evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 5F

claims.claim: Immature TLSs were found both adjacent and not adjacent to islets.
claims.source: We found immature TLSs both adjacent (Figure 5G.1) or not adjacent (Figure 5G.2) to islets.
claims.evidence: Direct observation from imaging data shown in Figure 5G

claims.claim: Fewer than half of the immature TLSs were adjacent to islets.
claims.source: Quantifying the frequency of this adjacency revealed that fewer than half of the immature TLSs were adjacent to islets (Figure 5H).
claims.evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 5H

claims.claim: No differences were identified in the cellular composition of the immature TLSs that were or were not adjacent to islets.
claims.source: We did not identify any differences in the cellular composition of the immature TLSs that were or were not adjacent to islets (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claims.claim: Islet-adjacent CD45RA+/CD8+T cells co-expressed CD62L, suggesting that they originated from the (CD8+T cells|B cell) CN.
claims.source: We reasoned that even if immature TLSs were far from islets, extravasating cells may migrate to islets. Accordingly, islet-adjacent CD45RA+/CD8+T cells (that were not in islet-adjacent TLSs) co-expressed CD62L, suggesting that they originated from the (CD8+T cells|B cell) CN (HH).
claims.evidence: Inference drawn from the co-expression of CD45RA and CD62L on islet-adjacent T cells

claims.claim: In one tissue donor, regions of the pancreas with Insulin-Depleted islets were enriched in the (CD8+T cells|B cell) CN relative to regions with β-cell containing islets.
claims.source: Consistent with this, in one notable tissue donor, regions of the pancreas with Insulin-Depleted islets were enriched in the (CD8+T cells|B cell) CN relative to regions of the pancreas with β-cell containing islets (Figure 5J).
claims.evidence: Direct observation from imaging data shown in Figure 5J

claims.claim: The spatial correlation between the (CD8+T cells|B cells) CN and the destruction of islets implicates immature TLSs with islet pathology even if they are not adjacent to islets.
claims.source: This spatial correlation between the (CD8+T cells|B cells) CN and the destruction of islets implicates immature TLSs with islet pathology even if they are not adjacent to islets (Figure 5J).
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from the spatial correlation shown in Figure 5J

claims.claim: The results are consistent with the model previously proposed by Damond et al, who proposed a single trajectory for insulitis, characterized by an enrichment in HLA-ABC expression, CD8+T cells, and macrophage/DCs.
claims.source: First, our results are consistent with the model previously proposed by Damond et al, who proposed a single trajectory for insulitis, characterized by an enrichment in HLA-ABC expression, CD8+T cells, and macrophage/DCs (Damond et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Comparison of current results with previous model, supported by citation to Damond et al., 2019

claims.claim: This is the first report that IDO+ vasculature is present in inflamed islets but not in normal islets or islets that have lost insulin-expression.
claims.source: Second, we are the first to report that IDO+ vasculature is present in inflamed islets but not in normal islets or islets that have lost insulin-expression (Figure 2G, Figure 2H).

results.result: The study used CODEX imaging with a 54-antigen antibody panel to analyze approximately 2000 islets from a cohort of 13 donors (2 AA+, 8 T1D, 3 non-T1D controls), generating a dataset of 7.0×10^6 cells. Twenty-one cell types were identified using Leiden clustering and manual merging.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C17 provide a comprehensive description of the study design, cohort composition, and analytical approach. The methodology is clearly stated with specific numbers for cohort size, imaging area, cell counts, and cell type identification. The cohort selection rationale (C12) is appropriately justified given the rarity of insulitis cases.

results.result: β-cell frequencies were significantly reduced in T1D patients with 0-2 years disease duration compared to controls, with minimal β-cell mass remaining in patients with 5-6 years duration. PCA analysis separated donors into distinct groups based on non-endocrine cell type abundances in both islet and extra-islet compartments.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C21 describe β-cell loss progression and cellular composition differences between T1D and control samples. The statistical findings (C18) and PCA separation (C20) are clearly stated with reference to figures. The conclusion that both compartments are distinct (C21) logically follows from the PCA results.

results.result: Pseudotime analysis using PAGA identified a single, non-branching trajectory of insulitis progression from Normal to Inflamed to Insulin-Depleted islets, characterized by increasing HLA-ABC expression, CD8+T cells, and macrophage/DCs. Immune cells specifically targeted islets as demonstrated by enrichment analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C27 describe the pseudotime reconstruction of islet pathogenesis. The methodology (PAGA) is appropriate for trajectory inference, and the three-stage classification (C24) is objectively defined using internal Leiden clustering. The spatial enrichment analysis (C26) provides strong evidence for islet-specific targeting. The consistency with prior work (C27) strengthens confidence in the findings.

results.result: IDO expression on islet vasculature was specifically associated with inflamed islets and correlated with increased CD8+T cell infiltration and elevated HLA-ABC expression in β-cells, but not with macrophage/DC abundance. This suggests IDO may function as an immunoregulatory checkpoint in T1D.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C36 describe a novel finding regarding IDO expression patterns. The observations are well-documented with specific localization (C29-C30), quantification (C31), and statistical associations (C33-C35). The conclusion that IDO is an immunoregulatory checkpoint (C36) is appropriately presented as speculative ('may be') given the correlative nature of the data.

results.result: High-dimensional spatial phenotyping using a neural network identified heterogeneous CD8+T cell activation profiles in islets, with four distinct inflamed islet sub-clusters (I-IV) characterized by different combinations of functional markers including CD45RA, CD45RO, PD-1, LAG-3, Granzyme-B, ICOS, and CD57.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C48 describe comprehensive CD8+T cell phenotyping. The neural network approach (C37) provides high-quality marker quantification, and the identification of four sub-clusters (C43-C47) is clearly documented with specific marker profiles. The conclusion of heterogeneous activation profiles (C42, C48) is well-supported by the data.

results.result: Insulitis sub-states are conserved across T1D patients, with each donor possessing islets from multiple sub-clusters. The specific CD8+T cell activation profiles characterizing each sub-cluster were enriched within islets compared to surrounding tissue and were independent of other cell type abundances.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C56 establish that insulitis sub-states are patient-independent but islet-specific. The observation that each donor has multiple sub-clusters (C49) rules out donor-level factors (C50). The spatial enrichment analysis (C52-C53) and lack of association with other cell types (C54-C56) are clearly demonstrated, though the mechanism remains unexplained.

results.result: Insulin-Depleted + Immune islets showed altered CD8+T cell composition compared to Inflamed islets, with higher frequencies of CD45RA+ and TOX+ T cells (which were never co-expressed), suggesting that the activation state or persistence of these populations depends on insulin expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C60 describe differences in T cell populations between Inflamed and Insulin-Depleted islets. The observations are clearly stated (C57-C59), and the conclusion about insulin-dependence (C60) is a reasonable inference from the data, though the mechanism is not established.

results.result: Lobular patterning of insulitis varies widely across T1D cases (ICC 0.17-0.74). Hierarchical linear modeling identified three extra-islet cell types (vasculature, nerves, Granzyme-B+/CD3- cells) significantly associated with lobules containing late-pseudotime islets, while CD8+T cells and macrophage/DCs were not associated with lobular patterning.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C71 describe lobular patterning analysis using appropriate statistical methods (HLM). The ICC quantification (C64-C65) demonstrates variability across cases. The identification of three associated cell types (C66-C69) is statistically supported, and the counterintuitive finding about CD8+T cells (C70) adds credibility. The speculative conclusion (C71) is appropriately cautious.

results.result: Cellular neighborhood analysis identified 75 CNs, with the top three enriched in T1D being (CD8+T cells|B cells), (Macrophage|Stromal Cells|B cells), and (Vasculature|B cells). The (CD8+T cells|B cells) CN was predominantly adjacent to the other two CNs but lacked segregated T and B cell zones characteristic of mature TLSs.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C78 describe cellular neighborhood identification and characterization. The methodology (C72) is clearly explained, and the identification of B cell-enriched CNs (C74) with specific spatial relationships (C75) is well-documented. The observation that these structures lack mature TLS features (C77) is appropriately noted.

results.result: The (CD8+T cells|B cells) CN represents immature TLSs based on the presence of PNAd+ HEVs and B cell aggregation without compartmentalized zones. CD45RA+/CD62L+/CD8+T cells were observed near PNAd+ vasculature, with CD45RA enriched threefold in this CN, suggesting these structures may support naive T cell entry into the pancreas.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C83 characterize the (CD8+T cells|B cells) CN as immature TLSs. The identification of HEVs (C79) and the classification as immature TLSs (C80) are appropriately based on established criteria. The observations of CD45RA+/CD62L+ T cells (C81, C83) support the hypothesis about T cell entry (C82), though this remains speculative.

results.result: Immature TLSs were found both adjacent and distant from islets, with fewer than half adjacent to islets. Islet-adjacent CD45RA+/CD62L+/CD8+T cells suggest migration from TLSs to islets. In one donor, regions with Insulin-Depleted islets were enriched in immature TLSs, implicating these structures in islet pathology even when not adjacent.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C89 describe the spatial relationship between immature TLSs and islets. The quantification of adjacency (C85) and lack of compositional differences (C86) are clearly stated. The inference about T cell migration (C87) is reasonable but speculative. The spatial correlation in one donor (C88-C89) provides suggestive but limited evidence for the role of distant TLSs.

results.result: The study confirms the single trajectory model of insulitis proposed by Damond et al. and reports the novel finding that IDO+ vasculature is present specifically in inflamed islets with higher CD8+T cell frequencies. The loss of IDO on vasculature could be a prerequisite for β-cell death, and leveraging this checkpoint has shown promise in transplantation studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C96 summarize key findings and place them in context. The consistency with prior work (C90) and novelty of the IDO finding (C91-C92) are clearly stated. The speculative conclusion about IDO loss (C93) is appropriately cautious. The discussion of IDO expression discrepancies (C95-C96) demonstrates critical evaluation of conflicting literature.

results.result: This study performed the first high-dimensional spatial phenotyping of CD8+T cells in T1D islets, finding that most T cells were antigen-experienced with heterogeneous populations including CD45RA+/CD69+ cells and LAG-3+/Granzyme-B+/ICOS+ cells. Only a small population of islets had Granzyme-B-expressing T cells, suggesting alternative β-cell elimination mechanisms may be involved.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C102 highlight the novelty and key findings of the T cell phenotyping. The claim of being 'first' (C97) is supported by the comprehensive marker panel and spatial resolution. The observations about T cell populations (C98-C101) are well-documented. The speculation about alternative mechanisms (C102) is appropriately cautious given the limited Granzyme-B expression.

results.result: The insulitis trajectory comprises four sub-clusters present in all T1D donors, with T cell activation profiles specific to the islet microenvironment. Lobules enriched in β-cell-depleted islets were also enriched in nerves, vasculature, and Granzyme-B+/CD3- cells (possibly CD56dim NK cells). The distinct cell types linked to islet invasion versus lobule patterning suggest crosstalk between compartments may be required for complete islet destruction.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C111 synthesize findings about insulitis sub-states and lobular patterning. The observations are well-supported by the data (C103-C107), and the speculation about NK cells (C108) is appropriately cautious. The conclusion about compartment crosstalk (C110) is a reasonable inference, though the therapeutic implication (C111) is speculative.

results.result: The study identified immature TLSs away from islets where CD45RA+/CD8+T cells aggregate, and an inflamed islet sub-cluster characterized by CD45RA+ T cells. Mouse studies showing that blocking lymph node egress reduced TLS size and halted diabetes suggest that therapeutic targeting of immune cell trafficking to TLSs could help mitigate human T1D autoimmunity.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C116 summarize TLS findings and therapeutic implications. The observations (C112-C113) are well-documented. The mouse data (C114) provides supporting evidence, though cross-species translation is uncertain. The therapeutic speculation (C115) is appropriately cautious. The summary statement (C116) accurately reflects the study's integrative approach.

results.result: The study has several limitations including small cohort size (due to rarity of insulitis cases), inability to balance confounding factors (drug use, ICU duration, BMI), limited AA+ cases with insulitis, failure to identify myeloid heterogeneity (likely due to segmentation difficulties), and use of 2D sections which could affect adjacency relations.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C124 provide an honest assessment of study limitations. The cohort size limitation (C117-C119) is appropriately justified by the rarity of insulitis cases. The AA+ case limitation (C120-C121) is clearly stated. The myeloid analysis limitation (C122-C123) acknowledges technical challenges. The 2D section limitation (C124) is a standard caveat for tissue imaging studies.

results.result: Using a data-driven approach, the study mapped conserved sub-states of insulitis and integrated the spatial pathology of islet and extra-islet regions into a single model of T1D pathogenesis. The tools and computational pipelines developed will enable further investigation of immune pathology at the tissue scale that may lead to therapies for T1D.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C126 provide appropriate summary statements. The claim about mapping sub-states and integrating compartments (C125) accurately reflects the study's achievements. The statement about future utility (C126) is appropriately speculative about therapeutic development while being confident about the methodological contributions.

results.result: The introduction establishes the clinical significance of T1D (affecting 8 million individuals with 0.5 million new diagnoses annually), the limited efficacy of current immunotherapies including teplizumab, and the availability of human pancreatic tissue through nPOD. Prior studies have documented increased extra-islet immune cells, elevated HLA-DR on ductal cells, peri-insulitis, variable islet infiltration rates, and TLSs in T1D patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C9 provide appropriate background context with proper citations. The epidemiological data (C1), therapeutic landscape (C2-C3), and tissue resource (C4) establish the study's rationale. The summary of prior extra-islet findings (C5-C9) appropriately motivates the study's focus on both compartments. All claims are supported by citations to relevant literature.

results.result: The study used CODEX imaging with a 54-antigen antibody panel to analyze approximately 2000 islets from a cohort of 13 donors (2 AA+, 8 T1D, 3 non-T1D controls), generating a dataset of 7.0×10^6 cells and identifying 21 cell types.
results.evaluation: All reviewers acknowledge the use of CODEX methodology and the cohort composition without criticism. Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'Major strengths of this study are the use of pancreas tissue from well-characterized tissue donors, the use of CODEX, a state-of-the-art detection technique.' The methodology is validated by the reviewers' acceptance of the findings derived from it.

results.result: T1D donors showed significantly reduced β-cell frequencies compared to non-T1D controls, with progressive β-cell loss correlating with disease duration. PCA analysis separated T1D and non-T1D cases based on both islet and extra-islet cellular composition.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings without challenge. Reviewer 3 notes 'By using their innovative imaging/computation approaches, key known features of islet autoimmunity were confirmed, providing validation of the methodology.' The progressive β-cell loss and distinct cellular profiles are treated as confirmatory evidence supporting the validity of the approach.

results.result: Pseudotime analysis identified a single, non-branching progression from Normal to Inflamed to Insulin-Depleted islets, characterized by elevated HLA-ABC expression, CD8+T cells, and macrophage/DCs in Inflamed islets, with immune cells specifically targeting islets.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly states 'the description of four sub-clusters characterized by the activation profile of the islet-infiltrating CD8+T cells is novel' and notes the results are 'consistent with the model previously proposed by Damond et al.' Reviewer 1 highlights this as a 'confirmatory observation' that validates the methodology. The progression model is accepted as robust.

results.result: IDO+ vasculature was specifically observed in inflamed islets but not in normal or insulin-depleted islets. IDO+ islets contained higher frequencies of CD8+T cells and elevated HLA-ABC expression, suggesting IDO may be an immunoregulatory checkpoint induced by T cell-derived cytokines.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 identifies 'the upregulation of indolamine 2,3-dioxygenase-1 in the islet microvasculature' as a 'notable finding.' Reviewer 3 states 'The detection of IDO+ vasculature in inflamed islets - but not in normal islets or islets that have lost insulin-expression links this expression to the islet inflammation, and it is a novel observation' and notes 'it may provide a potential therapeutic avenue.' All reviewers accept this finding without criticism.

results.result: High-dimensional spatial phenotyping using a neural network revealed that most islet-infiltrating CD8+T cells were antigen-experienced, expressing markers like PD-1, TOX, CD45RO, CD69, and CD44. Rare populations included CD45RA+ cells and cells co-expressing LAG-3, Granzyme-B, and ICOS.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 states 'The high-dimensional spatial phenotyping of CD8+T cells in T1D islets confirmed that most T cells were antigen experienced. Some additional subsets were noted' and describes this as novel. Reviewer 1 notes the study 'increases the resolution for linking these features with specific cellular subsets using machine learning algorithms.' The neural network approach and findings are accepted without methodological criticism.

results.result: Four inflamed islet sub-clusters (I-IV) were identified based on CD8+T cell activation profiles. These sub-clusters were present in all T1D donors and characterized by distinct marker expression patterns (CD45RA+ in Inflamed-II, CD45RO+/PD-1+ in Inflamed-III, and multiple activation markers in Inflamed-IV). The T cell phenotypes were specific to the islet microenvironment, not the surrounding tissue.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly states 'the description of four sub-clusters characterized by the activation profile of the islet-infiltrating CD8+T cells is novel. Their presence in all T1D donors, indicates that the disease process is asynchronous and is not at the same stage across all islets. Although this concept is not novel, this appears to be the most advanced characterization of insulitis stages.' The finding is treated as a major advance in understanding insulitis heterogeneity.

results.result: The activation states of islet-infiltrating CD8+T cells were independent of macrophage/DC abundance, IDO expression, or any other cell type identified in the study.
results.evaluation: This finding is not explicitly discussed by reviewers but is implicitly accepted as part of the overall characterization of CD8+T cell heterogeneity. No reviewer challenges the independence of T cell states from other cellular factors, and the finding supports the novel characterization of insulitis sub-states that reviewers explicitly praise.

results.result: Insulin-Depleted islets showed different CD8+T cell compositions compared to Inflamed islets, with higher frequencies of CD45RA+ and TOX+ T cells (which never co-expressed), suggesting that T cell activation or persistence depends on insulin expression.
results.evaluation: This finding is part of the overall characterization of T cell heterogeneity that Reviewer 3 describes as 'the most advanced characterization of insulitis stages.' The relationship between insulin expression and T cell phenotypes is accepted as part of the progression model without specific criticism.

results.result: Lobular patterning analysis revealed that lobules with advanced insulitis were enriched in vasculature, nerves, and Granzyme-B+/CD3- cells in the extra-islet space. The magnitude of lobular patterning varied widely (ICC 0.17-0.74) across T1D cases. Notably, CD8+T cells and macrophage/DCs were not associated with lobular patterning despite being elevated in T1D extra-islet compartments.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 states 'When examining together both the exocrine and islet areas, which is rarely done, authors report that pancreatic lobules affected by insulitis are characterized by distinct tissue markers. Their data support the concept that disease progression may require crosstalk between cells in the islet and extra-islet compartments.' The finding that cell types linked to islet invasion differ from those linked to lobular patterning is accepted as novel insight.

results.result: Cellular neighborhood analysis identified 75 CNs, with the top three enriched in T1D being (CD8+T cells|B cells), (Macrophage|Stromal Cells|B cells), and (Vasculature|B cells). The (CD8+T cells|B cells) CN showed characteristics of immature TLSs, including PNAd+ HEVs but lacking segregated T and B cell zones, and was more abundant in early T1D (0-2 years duration).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes the study 'provide key insights as to the cell:cell interactions within organ donors, again supporting a previously reported interaction between presumably autoreactive T and B cells.' Reviewer 3 states 'authors report that immature tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) exist both near and away from islets, where CD45RA+ CD8+T cells aggregate...These TLSs may represent a point of entry for T cells and this study further supports their role in islet autoimmunity.' The characterization is accepted as advancing understanding of TLS involvement.

results.result: CD45RA+/CD62L+/CD8+T cells were observed near PNAd+ vasculature in immature TLSs, with CD45RA+ enriched threefold in these structures. Immature TLSs were found both adjacent and distant from islets (fewer than half adjacent), and spatial correlation between TLSs and insulin-depleted islets was observed in one donor, implicating TLSs in islet pathology even when not adjacent.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly accepts this finding, stating 'Lastly, authors report that immature tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) exist both near and away from islets, where CD45RA+ CD8+T cells aggregate, and also observed an inflamed islet-subcluster characterized by an abundance of CD45RA+/CD8+ T cells.' The spatial relationship and potential role of TLSs as entry points for T cells is accepted without challenge.

results.result: The study acknowledges major limitations including small cohort size (only 17 of ~200 nPOD T1D cases had documented insulitis), inability to balance or adjust for confounding factors (drug use, ICU duration, BMI), and limited representation of the AA+ preclinical stage (only one of two AA+ cases had detectable insulitis).
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly acknowledge the cohort size limitation. Reviewer 1 states 'the data are still limited in terms of subject numbers - a challenge in a disease characterized by extensive heterogeneity.' Reviewer 2 states 'A major limitation of the study is the cohort size, which the authors directly state.' Reviewer 3 notes 'the major limitation is that the number of donors examined is limited' and discusses the impact on examining disease heterogeneity and age at diagnosis. The limitation is universally recognized but accepted given the rarity of suitable samples.

results.result: The study failed to identify heterogeneity in myeloid populations during insulitis, likely due to difficulty in segmenting myeloid cells and quantifying marker expression due to their morphology.
results.evaluation: This limitation is acknowledged by the authors and implicitly accepted by reviewers. Reviewer 1 notes 'the study does present a rich and integrated dataset for analysis of enriched immune markers' but also acknowledges the immune-focused nature may miss other aspects. The limitation is treated as a technical challenge rather than a fundamental flaw.

results.result: Prior literature establishes that T1D is characterized by increased extra-islet immune cells, elevated HLA-DR on ductal cells, peri-insulitis, heterogeneous islet infiltration rates across pancreatic regions, presence of TLSs, and asynchronous β-cell destruction across islets.
results.evaluation: These claims represent established background knowledge cited from prior literature. Reviewers accept these as context without challenge. Reviewer 3 notes 'Although this concept is not novel' regarding asynchronous disease progression, confirming these are accepted features of T1D pathology that provide context for the novel findings.

results.result: The study integrated spatial pathology of islet and extra-islet regions into a single model of T1D pathogenesis using data-driven approaches, with tools and pipelines that may enable future investigations and therapeutic development.
results.evaluation: The Editor's assessment states the study 'identify a series of intriguing "immune signatures" and histopathological features that collectively constitute a solid foundation for future investigations into immunological processes underpinning the pathogenesis of T1D.' Reviewer 3 states 'The study expands the conceptual framework of inflammation and islet autoimmunity, especially by the definition of different clusters (stages) of insulitis and by the characterization of immune cells in and outside the islets.' The integrative approach is recognized as a major contribution.
